title: Research on Financial Stock Market Prediction Based on the Hidden Quantum Markov Model
abstract_summary: The paper addresses HQMM's inability to handle continuous financial time series by introducing a GMM-MVTF discretization pipeline that converts continuous stock data into discrete sequences. It develops and evaluates HQMM variants on 15 SSE and SZSE stocks (2018–2021), showing that HQMM with MVTF-discretized data outperforms classical HMM and evenly-discretized HQMM in predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and practical applicability for market-regime forecasting and portfolio decision support.
methodology_description: The study develops a quantum-inspired forecasting pipeline that applies Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HQMM) to stock market trend prediction. Fifteen stocks from the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges (daily OHLCV) for June 2018–June 2021 were collected via the Tushare API. Because HQMM requires discrete observations, the paper compares two discretization strategies: (1) simple even-binning of day-to-day price-change magnitudes into labeled states, and (2) a GMM+MVTF pipeline in which rolling 30-day slices are fit with a Gaussian Mixture Model (EM) to extract component means/variances, which are then transformed into a scalar L via a weighted sum (Formula 8) and mapped to discrete trend states via thresholds (Table 3). HQMM training maximizes the log-likelihood (Equation 9) with respect to Kraus operators subject to quantum channel constraints (sum_m K_m^† K_m = I). For optimization the authors stack Kraus operators into a matrix Z (on the Stiefel manifold) and perform constrained gradient descent using a matrix-update formula (Wen & Yin style) to obtain Kraus operators, update the density matrix ρ and evaluate the Description Accuracy (DA) metric for convergence (DA typically converges by ~40 iterations). Predictions are produced by computing J_n = -ln tr(K_n ρ_t K_n^†) for each observation operator and selecting the minimal J_n as the next discrete state; a simple backtest trading rule (buy for predicted rising-state labels, short for falling-state labels) is applied to compute final capital (FC) and comparative growth rate R = (FC - NC) / FC. The HQMM (with MVTF discretization) is evaluated against classical HMM and HQMM with even discretization across multiple prediction horizons (90/180/360 days) and reported in terms of DA, average final capital, average R, runtime and computational-scaling characteristics.

dataset_used: 15 individual stocks from the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE) and Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE), daily open/high/low/close/volume for the period June 2018 to June 2021. Data accessed via the Tushare API and processed with pandas/NumPy.
experiment_input: Source: Tushare API (SSE & SZSE). Items: daily OHLCV for 15 tickers (codes: 000901, 000036, 000031, 601318, 600519, 600009, 600004, 600050, 600022, 000623, 000401, 000488, 000518, 000800, 000895) covering Jun 2018–Jun 2021. Train/validation/test splits: train 2018-06-01 to 2019-10-26, validation 2019-10-30 to 2020-08-24, test 2020-08-24 to 2021-06-23. Preprocessing: compute daily price-change (close_t+1 - close_t), group data into 30-day windows for GMM fitting; two discretization options: (a) even discretization bins mapped to integer observation labels, (b) GMM (K empirically 5 or 6 in paper; EM used) to get component means/variances then MVTF mapping (Formula 8) to discrete state labels.
experiment_process: 1) Data collection via Tushare; 2) Preprocessing: compute daily change, slice into 30-day windows for GMM; 3) Discretization: either even-binning into state labels or GMM+MVTF mapping from component means/variances to scalar L and then to discrete states per Table 3; 4) HQMM model construction: choose number of hidden states (authors used 6 after global tuning), initialize density matrix ρ0 (example numeric vector provided); 5) Stack Kraus operators into matrix Z (dimension reported as 12×2 in experiments); 6) Maximize log-likelihood (Equation 9) subject to ∑ K_m^† K_m = I using constrained gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold (compute gradient G = ∂ζ/∂Z, update Z via Wen & Yin style formula with step-size τ); 7) Repeat until DA converges (fast increase for iterations <5, convergence by ~40 iterations); 8) Recover Kraus operators from Z, perform prediction per time-step by computing J_n = -ln tr(K_n ρ_t K_n^†) and selecting argmin J_n as predicted discrete state; 9) Backtest trading rule (initial capital IC = 1,000,000 CNY, buy for predicted rising states {2,4,6}, short for falling states {1,3,5}, no transaction costs) to compute final capital FC and comparative growth rate R; 10) Compare HQMM (MVTF & even) versus classical HMM across horizons 90/180/360 days. Key iteration behavior: DA improves quickly <5 iterations and plateaus by ~40 iterations.
experiment_output: Outputs and metrics: Description Accuracy (DA) as the standardized log-likelihood evaluation for trained models; backtest outputs final capital (FC) per strategy and comparative growth rate R = (FC - NC) / FC relative to natural (buy-and-hold) growth NC. Baselines: classical HMM and HQMM with even discretization. Reported aggregate results include average capital across 15 stocks, average R (%), total runtime (minutes), and qualitative computational-complexity statements (HMM O(T n^2), HQMM O(T n w)). Also reported intermediate outputs: learned Kraus matrices and DA convergence curves.

results_summary: The authors developed a GMM+MVTF discretization pipeline to convert continuous stock time series into discrete observations for Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HQMM). They trained HQMMs on 15 Chinese equities (2018–2021) and compared two HQMM variants (even discretization vs. GMM+MVTF) to a classical HMM baseline. Empirically, HQMM with GMM+MVTF produced the highest average final capital (1,404,827 CNY) and comparative growth rate (4.96%), outperforming both classical HMM (final capital 1,390,860 CNY, R=3.73%) and HQMM with even discretization (final capital 1,362,922 CNY, R=1.59%). Training/processing time reported for HQMM variants was 12 minutes versus 40 minutes for HMM on the authors' setup. The authors argue these results show a practical advantage of a quantum-inspired HQMM approach when combined with careful discretization, while also presenting theoretical claims about quantum-coherent advantages and scalability.

DA training behavior for HQMM: rapid DA increase in first ~5 iterations and convergence by ~40 iterations (plots shown in paper).
Discretization cluster parameter for GMM set empirically to n = 6 (authors' experiments used n = 5 in some descriptions; the paper indicates n≥1 and empirical choices).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper attributes improved forecasting performance to HQMM (a quantum-inspired model) and describes theoretical quantum advantages (coherence, interference, entanglement, and favorable scaling). However, experiments were conducted with classical implementations/optimizations of HQMM and limited empirical scope (15 stocks, single dataset, specific discretization pipeline). No demonstration on quantum hardware or comprehensive ablation studies isolate a genuine quantum-computational advantage, so claims of quantum advantage remain suggestive/speculative rather than conclusively demonstrated.
limitations: HQMM cannot be applied directly to continuous financial data and therefore required a bespoke discretization pipeline (GMM + MVTF) to be usable on the tested problems.
Data preprocessing has bottlenecks for high-frequency markets (author-stated).
Transaction costs, market impact and execution frictions were neglected in the backtesting (author-stated in methods).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — HQMM with GMM-MVTF discretization achieves higher Description Accuracy and better backtest final capital/R versus classical HMM and HQMM with even discretization on 15 SSE/SZSE stocks across 90/180/360-day horizons.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The HQMM pipeline is implemented and trained classically (Kraus-operator parametrization, Stiefel-manifold constrained gradient descent) showing practical applicability without requiring quantum hardware.
#idea:quantum-advantage — Authors claim computational-scaling benefits (HQMM O(T n w) vs HMM O(T n^2)), arguing improved runtime and scalability for the HQMM formulation.

#limitation:data-encoding — HQMM requires discrete observations; the proposed GMM+MVTF discretization adds preprocessing complexity and may introduce information loss or hyperparameter sensitivity (GMM components, window size, thresholds).
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments are classical implementations/simulations (no QPU/real-hardware results), so no empirical quantum speedup or hardware validation is provided.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Training behavior is reported as efficient (DA rises quickly <5 iterations and typically converges by ~40 iterations) and authors provide code/data for reproducibility.
contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — Paper reports HQMM 'quantum' superiority over classical HMM, but the experiments are classical implementations/simulations of HQMM (no QPU/hardware). Therefore the observed gains may stem from model expressiveness or improved discretization rather than any demonstrated quantum computational advantage.

contradiction:scalability — The paper claims improved computational scaling analytically, yet empirical evaluation is limited to 15 individual stocks and small model sizes; the claimed scalability to larger universes or higher-dimensional problems is not empirically validated.
